newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grain - Prices soft on ample stocks.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Prices soft on ample stocks.

text.p: Domestic corn prices in Indonesia will probably remain weak because of the ongoing harvest in the Lampung district of South Sumatra, while high stocks will keep prices weak in Thailand and Malaysia, traders said on Wednesday.

A trader in the key growing area of Lampung said she had been getting about 150 tonnes of corn a day compared with one-third that amount a couple of weeks ago. She added that arrivals were expected to rise to about 1,000 tonnes a day during the December/January peak.
"I expect prices to weaken further as the harvest picks up," she added.
A Jakarta-based trader said he expected the cancellation of some imported corn contracts for second quarter, 1997 arrival which were ordered when prices were relatively high.
"I have been hearing that some players bought corn at US$160-$163 C&F (a tonne), which are much higher than current prices. I see the chances of one or two Panamaxes being cancelled," he said.
The trader also attributed the possible cancellations to the local harvest and ample stocks.
He expected the cancellations to come from traders, while end-users were likely to stick by their contracts.
Corn was quoted at 395-400 rupiah a kg in Jakarta, compared with 400-405 rupiah a week ago. Soymeal was around 800 rupiah a kg, down from 800-810 rupiah.
A trader said he expected 90,000 tonnes of soymeal to arrive this month, with about 100,000 tonnes arriving in December, mostly from India.
In Thailand, corn prices were steady to lower at 4.28-4.40 baht a kg from 4.30-4.40 baht a kg last week as some feed producers and poultry farmers turned to cheaper broken rice as a substitute.
Many Thai buyers, however, sat it out on the sidelines in anticipation prices will come down further, trade sources said.

Except for the purchase of 50,000 tonnes of soybeans by oil crushers recently for January shipment, there have been no new buying orders, they said. The beans were reportedly bought at between $291-$295 a tonne C&F Bangkok.
One major feed producer was said to have sought a cargo of soymeal for prompt shipment at $300 a tonne C&F Bangkok.
"But no deal was made because the prices were quoted by traders above that level," one trader said.
The U.S.-origin soymeal for January shipment was quoted around $318 a tonne C&F Bangkok while Indian origin meal was quoted at about $308 on the same basis, trade sources said.
"The supply at the moment is enough to cover this year's demand. Buyers are not under pressure to buy. I believe if soybean prices dropped a bit further, buyers would emerge," a trader said.
Although local soymeal stocks are diminishing, prices eased due to the influx of imports. Soymeal was quoted around 9.20-9.50 baht a kg from 9.60 baht a kg last week.
"The removal of the import quota on soybean and soymeal which went into effect on November 1 also pressured prices," another importer said.
Malaysian prices were unchanged this week as buyers stayed sidelined following signs Chicago futures may turn around after several weeks of falls.
"The futures market could be rebounding soon and local buyers are still uncertain of how sharp the rise could be," said a trader with a a flour mill in Kuala Lumpur.
"Everyone seems to be assessing the situation for the moment and being cautious of buying," added the trader.
Another dealer said it could take another week before substantial buying would be seen in the local market.
"I think by next week we'll have a pretty good idea where the Chicago market is headed," said the dealer.
Traders could not report any significant off-take for the week, saying Malaysian consumers were technically well-stocked until the first quarter of next year.
Bulk corn for December was being offered at 475 to 480 ringgit a tonne ex-factory/godown in the central region.
"A" grade wheat in bags was at 800 ringgit a tonne ex-factory/godown in the central region. Low-grade wheat was steady at 500-510 ringgit a tonne.
Local soymeal was quoted at 810 ringgit a tonne while imported soymeal was indicated at 800 ringgit a tonne.
